papers.title: Revisiting Elliptic++ for Bitcoin Forensics: Feature Reconstruction and Leakage-Resistant Evaluation
papers.abstract: Elliptic and its address-level extension Elliptic++ are widely used benchmark datasets in Bitcoin forensics, cited by more than 1300 academic studies according to Google Scholar. We identify future information leakage in Elliptic++. Its positional data split does not respect temporal order, and the exact definitions of its address-level features remain undocumented. We revisit how the 55 Elliptic++ address-level features are computed and propose a leakage-resistant pipeline. First, the exact feature definitions are recovered by linking Elliptic transactions to public ledger data. Second, we compute the features with a temporal split based on each address's first appearance, using only information available at the time of prediction. Once temporal ordering is enforced, the random forest (RF)'s strong predictive performance largely disappears: its F1 score on the illicit class falls from $0.846$ under the original leaky evaluation to just $0.291$ under our leakage-resistant pipeline. Furthermore, RF no longer outperforms a simple logistic regression baseline. We provide the exact feature definitions and executable code to reproduce the leakage-resistant features, so that future Bitcoin forensic models can be evaluated based on genuine predictive capability rather than temporal data leakage.

papers.title: Regret-based Characterization, Information Limits, and the Sample Complexity of Auditing Adaptive Policies
papers.abstract:
A policy can earn its performance by where it locates on average or by reacting to information. For any Markov policy $\pi$ in a finite-horizon MDP, let $
u$ be its open-loop marginal, which plays $\pi$'s average action distribution at each step. We show that $J(\pi)-J(
u)$ equals $\sum_t tr Cov(Q^
u_t,\pi_t)$ under endogenous dynamics. Audits based on immediate costs alone can have the wrong sign. Writing the covariance as a joint-versus-product gap gives the bound $|J(\pi)-J(
u)|\le\sum_t span_t\sqrt{I(s_t;a_t)/2}$, with a sharp constant. Hence, an MDP's adaptivity gap is bounded by the information that its optimal policy uses. Estimating $J(\pi)-J(
u)$ from $\pi$'s own bandit-feedback logs takes $\Theta( ar\chi^2 \log(1/\eta)/\delta^2)$ rounds, where $ ar\chi^2$ is an average $\chi^2$-divergence. At the same time, deterministic non-constant policies cannot be audited at all. We also provide an importance-sampling auditor for episodic MDPs.

papers.title: PanelGP: A Probabilistic Factor Model for Asset-Return Panels
papers.abstract: We develop PanelGP, a conditional factor model for large panels of stock returns in which firm characteristics determine the factor loadings and economic conditions determine the expected factors. Both relations are estimated nonparametrically with Gaussian-process priors. The kernel choice nests instrumented principal component analysis (IPCA) as well as smooth nonlinear maps. Asset-specific loading innovations and common factor innovations separate idiosyncratic from systematic risk, so one estimated model forecasts both expected returns and their covariance matrix. Estimation uses sparse variational inference with a joint posterior over loadings and factors. Because each predicted return is bilinear in a Gaussian state, the predictive covariance matrix and the cumulants of any portfolio have closed forms. In simulations, the estimator recovers the nonlinear maps and the variance parameters. For S&P 500 constituents over 1995-2024, nonlinear loadings rank stocks better than affine loadings and improve the Gaussian log score. Relative to IPCA, the resulting portfolios have higher Sharpe ratios, also net of trading costs, and the minimum-variance portfolio has lower volatility. The predicted variances rank stocks and months by risk but are too compressed.

papers.title: When Listwise Deletion Works: Causal Diagrams and Complete-Case Regression
papers.abstract: Listwise deletion (LWD) appears more common than imputation: our review of leading journals finds that about 50% of articles state or imply LWD, versus 7% describing an imputation model. Assuming oracle regression with all required values observed consistently estimates the population average treatment effect, we ask when complete-case regression remains consistent. With constant effects, we offer two checks: whether covariates and the missing indicator satisfy the adjustment criterion in an augmented causal diagram (DAG), and whether the estimator pools valid within-covariate comparisons appropriately, potentially using inverse treatment-propensity weighting (IPW). For heterogeneous effects, assuming conditional effects carry over to the population, we reweight comparisons to the population covariate distribution. Simulations and empirical illustrations from American politics, comparative politics, and international relations demonstrate the framework's use and show why a missing-at-random (MAR) classification, although useful for assessing imputation, does not by itself establish whether complete-case regression consistently estimates the target population ATE. Thus, we recommend adding the missing indicator and its causes to causal models, then checking adjustment and weighting for LWD.

papers.title: Refining the Notion of No Anticipation in Difference-in-Differences Studies
papers.abstract: We clarify the interpretation of identification strategies using difference-in-differences (DiD), which are widely applied in empirical research. In particular, DiD researchers often invoke an assumption commonly referred to as the "no-anticipation assumption". Taken literally, this assumption states that treatments in the future have no effect on outcomes in the past. Because standard causal models rely on a temporal structure in which causes precede effects, such an assumption seems to be inherently satisfied. However, most researchers attribute a different meaning to the assumption: they interpret the assumption as ensuring no effect of policy decision, e.g., immediate behavioral changes due to knowledge about the plan to implement the policy. We discuss the consequences of this mismatch, and give an alternative formulation of no anticipation that captures DiD researchers' concerns and clarifies identification arguments.

papers.title: Regression Discontinuity Approaches to Evaluate Threshold-Guided Interventions in Observational Studies
papers.abstract: This article provides an introduction to the Regression Discontinuity (RD) design, and its application to empirical research in the medical sciences. While the main focus of this article is on causal interpretation, key concepts of estimation and inference are also briefly mentioned. A running medical empirical example is provided.

papers.title: Logit-based alternatives to two-stage least squares
papers.abstract: We propose logit-based IV and augmented logit-based IV estimators that serve as alternatives to the traditionally used 2SLS estimator in the model where both the endogenous treatment variable and the corresponding instrument are binary. Our novel estimators are as easy to compute as the 2SLS estimator but have an advantage over the 2SLS estimator in terms of causal interpretability. In particular, in certain cases where the probability limits of both our estimators and the 2SLS estimator take the form of weighted-average treatment effects, our estimators are guaranteed to yield non-negative weights whereas the 2SLS estimator is not.

papers.title: Partially identified heteroskedastic SVARs
papers.abstract: This paper studies the identification of Structural Vector Autoregressions (SVARs) exploiting a break in the variances of the structural shocks. Point-identification for this class of models relies on an eigen-decomposition involving the covariance matrices of reduced-form errors and requires that all the eigenvalues are distinct. This point-identification, however, fails in the presence of multiplicity of eigenvalues. This occurs in an empirically relevant scenario where, for instance, only a subset of structural shocks had the break in their variances, or where a group of variables shows a variance shift of the same amount. Together with zero or sign restrictions on the structural parameters and impulse responses, we derive the identified sets for impulse responses and show how to compute them. We perform inference on the impulse response functions, building on the robust Bayesian approach developed for set identified SVARs. To illustrate our proposal, we present an empirical example based on the literature on the global crude oil market where the identification is expected to fail due to multiplicity of eigenvalues.

papers.title: Heterogeneous Treatment Effects via Dynamic Panel Data Methods
papers.abstract: We study dynamic panel data methods in a causal framework where treatment effects are heterogeneous and history-dependent. Sequential exchangeability alone does not guarantee that a first-differenced instrumental-variable (IV) estimand is a convex average of current effects, even if those effects are constant. We characterize additional conditions that are sufficient and necessary for eliminating trend contamination and guaranteeing a convex representation uniformly over compatible distributions of potential outcomes and treatments. Next, for a model with autoregressive untreated potential outcomes, we propose a conditional first-differenced IV regression that identifies the average treatment effect on the first-time treated without sequential exchangeability. Finally, we compare sequential exchangeability and parallel trends under sequential randomization and forward-looking treatment choices with learning, and show that, when treatments depend on recent outcomes, equal pre-treatment trends can coexist with violations of parallel trends.

papers.title: Identification, estimation and inference in Panel Vector Autoregressions using external instruments
papers.abstract: This paper proposes an identification inspired by the SVAR-IV literature that uses external instruments to identify panel vector autoregressions (PVARs), and discusses associated issues of identification, estimation, and inference. I introduce a form of local average treatment effect, the $\mu$-LATE, which arises when a continuous instrument targets a policy variable with linear effects, and which reduces to the local average treatment effect when the policy and the instrument are binary. Under standard assumptions of independence, exclusion, and monotonicity, I show that externally instrumented PVARs estimate the $\mu$-LATE. I construct confidence sets for the impulse responses based on the Anderson-Rubin statistic and, with several instruments, on conditional likelihood ratio tests, which are robust to weak instruments and to common shocks across units. I apply the method to the effect of stock market wealth on local labor markets across US counties.

papers.title: Model Selection in High-Dimensional Linear Regression using Boosting with Multiple Testing
papers.abstract: This paper studies model selection in high dimensional regression settings. We propose a Boosting with Multiple Testing (BMT) approach designed to address proxy signal contamination in environments with strongly correlated regressors, including settings driven by latent common factors. At each stage, at most one regressor is selected conditional on those already included, using a multiple testing threshold for the remaining candidates. Under stated dependence, detectability and design conditions, BMT recovers the exact true model with probability approaching one. A separate extension permits growing signal counts under additional restrictions. For fixed numbers of signals and proxies, we also establish recovery of an approximating model containing all true signals and no noise variables under a separate set of conditions. Following exact selection, fixed dimensional least squares has the oracle asymptotic distribution under the stated moment conditions. A theoretical comparison identifies designs and tuning sequences for which BMT is consistent while the Lasso is not. In the main Monte Carlo comparison, BMT has the highest median Matthews correlation coefficient and exact recovery rate and the lowest median coefficient root mean squared error among the compared specifications. Applications to U.S. emissions and inflation show that BMT combines sparse specifications with favourable forecast performance, including the lowest emissions forecasting errors in the reported comparisons and the best one quarter ahead forecasts in the baseline inflation comparison.

papers.title: Sharp Identification for Regressions with Interval-Observed and Missing Covariates
papers.abstract: Researchers frequently estimate regressions when key variables are missing or observed only through intervals. Imputation or assumptions about the observation process can yield seemingly precise but misleading conclusions. We develop methods for identification and inference that remain robust to such incomplete data. For a broad class of conditional moment models, we characterize the sharp identified set, the set of all parameter values consistent with the observed data and maintained regression model, without restricting how incomplete observations arise. We establish Hausdorff-consistent estimation and uniformly valid confidence regions, and develop computationally tractable implementations for common regression models. In an application relating interval-elicited discount rates to on-time high-school graduation, conventional inference excludes zero, whereas our interval-data-robust confidence regions include it. Exploiting sharp identification nevertheless yields substantially tighter confidence regions than non-sharp alternatives.
